newsitem.title: UK: UK-China, India cargo rates rise but dip elsewhere.
newsitem.headline: UK-China, India cargo rates rise but dip elsewhere.

text.p: The near total elimination of air cargo fuel surcharges coupled with a general lull in customer demand has cut the cost of airfreight from Britain to most Asia, Australasia and Mideast markets, a Reuters survey shows.

The removal of surcharges which lasted some five months has had a direct impact on the "bottom line" cost to shippers although some airlines have marked their formal tariffs higher hoping to minimise the decline in cash flow.

Despite the introduction by many airlines of these official traditional spring price rises, downward pressure on marketplace rates has also resulted from the introduction of extra summer timetable capacity tipping the balance against weak demand on some routes.

The two notable exceptions to this trend have been China and India, to which both ex-UK volumes and yields have been highly encouraging, while business to Hong Kong is also good, airlines and forwarders stated.
But Korea and Australia have been hit harder than most and there appears to be little prospect of an upturn in airfreight prospects to these markets in the foreseeable future, they added.
"After a quiet February and March, our business to China is now booming," said Ashraf Salama, of Jet Link, UK cargo general sales agent for China Eastern Airlines.

Jet Link has to truck cargo to Brussels to connect with a weekly China Eastern 60-tonne capacity MD-ll freighter service to Shanghai and to Amsterdam to tranship cargo onto twice-weekly CEA passenger MD-11 flights to the two Chinese cities.
"But even though we are offline in the UK, we are now getting a lot of enquiries for these services," said Salama, adding that bookings were split about 70/30 Shanghai/Beijing.
A similar upbeat attitude was expressed by Air China's UK cargo GSA Pace Airline Services, whose Mark Reith noted: "For air cargo, China is pretty buoyant at the moment."
At the beginning of this year the market dipped in the wake of import tax changes imposed by Beijing on machinery.
"But business has certainly picked up of late, for freight shipments of all kinds, particularly textiles from and to the UK," he said.
With the introduction of a new frequency on April 1, Air China is now offering 100 tonnes' space a week on two 747 Combi and one 747-200 passenger services London Heathrow-Beijing.

"Last year we were limited to just two weekly flights -- one with a Combi and the other with a limited capacity 747SP -- and yet London was still confirmed as the airline's best performing overseas cargo market," Reith said.
An Air France cargo spokesman in London described China as "a very good, always very healthy" market for the carrier in the UK, with the majority of shipments bound for Shanghai, follwed by Beijing.

Despite fierce competition on the UK-India route, Air India's UK cargo manager Madhav Lokur said this market was presently "booming". This is reflected in average ex-London per kg/100 kg rates increasing to both Bombay and Delhi over the past fortnight.

But the reverse is the case with UK-South Korea. Korean Air Lines' UK cargo sales manager Frank Smith said "The Korean economy has slowed down and there has also been a cutback in the purchase of luxury goods by Koreans,"
"The result has been that the ex-UK market, which was booming last year, has dropped right back -- and so have rates."
Smith lamented the introduction on Thursday of a new twice-weekly 747 freighter service from Manchester to Seoul and Kansai by Polar Air Cargo. "This will hit us," he said.

Another competitor is Asiana Airlines, which operates twice-weekly, 40-tonne capacity 747-400 Combi services from Brussels to Seoul and a weekly 747-400 freighter flight, capable of uplifting 100 tonnes, from Amsterdam Schiphol.
Cargo is trucked over to the Continent from the UK, where Mark Bright, of Asiana's UK cargo GSA Air Cargo Partners, said that his business to Korea had fallen over the past two weeks.
But in contrast to KAL, he described the overall state of the London-Seoul route as "pretty buoyant".
Malaysian Airline System's UK cargo manager Shahid Mir, however, said: "Business to Korea has dropped quite a lot recently."
There has certainly been some generous spot rating in this market recently, always a sign of some desperation to fill space, analysts said.
These go down to quotes of around 95 pence per kg for shipments of five or six tonnes and 1.25 stg per kg for one-tonne plus.
As for the UK-Australia, air cargo trading is also on a downward spiral, Reuters' research indicates.
"Volumes have dropped and so have the 'phone calls," said Keith O'Calaghan, UK cargo manager of Philippine Airlines .

While he said he "can't put a finger on the reason why", he felt that aggressive pricing on the Australia route being practised by British Airways had not helped to keep yields at a reasonable level while demand was down.
"Because of BA's pricing, I did not put my UK-Australia rates up from April 1," he added.
MAS' Mir said that while he was also aware of BA's pricing policy, "regardless, we have increased our London-Australia rates from five to seven percent" from the beginning of this month.
"I would describe the state of this market at present as reasonably stable," he said.

Cathay Pacific Airways' north UK cargo manager Ivor Llewellyn noted that while UK-Australia rates had generally been falling, he was obliged to keep his as published -- or otherwise be refused space from the airline's Hong Kong head office.
"The fact is that the average per kg yield for shipments to Australia from Japan is 1.5 times what it is from the UK," he stated.
"We can't drop our rates and we deal with (British) forwarders who are prepared to pay what we charge," he said.
Because of the fall in the Korean market, KAL's Smith said he was obliged to sell more to Australia where he felt he had found a niche in an increasingly low-cost market.
"While there is plenty of bellyhold capacity on the route, there are not many freighters offering main-deck capacity that can cope with heavy machinery shipments," he explained.
So he was taking advantage of KAL's new weekly, 65-tonne capacity MD-11 freighter service which was launched between Seoul and Sydney on April 2.
"I'm now selling that in the UK and it's going quite well," he said.
To Japan, the market is described as "reasonably good" by Asiana's Bright, whose GSA Air Cargo Partners also represents Polar in Britain.
But he does not anticipate much Japan business for either this U.S. carrier or Asiana -- or indeed any other flying the route -- in the seven days starting April 29.
This is Japan's 'Golden Week' when industries virtually come to a halt as the country celebrates a holiday period.
While ex-UK rates have dropped to most other Asia/Pacific destinations, to Hong Kong they have remained steady despite the entry of newcomer Air China on the route from March 31.
"Business during January-March was higher in terms of tonnage than it normally is at that time of the year," said Cathay's Llewellyn.
"Demand is showing signs of easing -- why, I don't know -- but I would say the market is still quite buoyant," he added.
He forecast that rather than taking long-standing custom away from direct operator Cathay, Air China would instead win traffic that to date has moved UK-HK via various transhipment routings.
Air China is operating a weekly Heathrow-HK service with a 747-200 passenger aircraft that can carry 22 tonnes of freight.
"There has been a lot of interest and every flight has so far gone full. We could sell the service 10 times over," said Reith, of the carrier's GSA Pace.
He added that "although nothing has been set in stone", there had been talk at Air China of a second weekly frequency on the UK-HK route, which he would welcome.

Unlike Hong Kong, the London-Manila market is showing signs of a slight decline. "It is not as buoyant as it was not so long ago and has especially gone a bit quiet over the past 10 days," said PAL's O'Callaghan.
"There is no particular reason for this trend and I am doing my best to be optimistic. I'm certainly not panicking," he stressed.
The Philippines is a market which Qatar Airways hopes to start selling soon from Britain, said its UK cargo manager John Curd.

But he said the carrier sees more potential in Thailand, which is served onward from the airline's new four-times-weekly, 10-tonne capacity Airbus A300-600R Heathrow-Doha services launched on March 31.
"We have not really got into selling Thailand, or Manila or Sri Lanka, from the UK yet, but we soon will," said Curd.
"We are especially excited about Bangkok, which will also be served by A300-600R aircraft, as apart from general cargo we will also be going into the courier business here," he added.

Elsewhere in South-east Asia, the ex-UK to Malaysia market is described as "reasonably healthy" by MAS' Mir, although he said business was presently a bit quieter now than it was at the same time in 1996.
While he sells onward from Kuala Lumpur, he said Singapore was not among his list of priorities. "It is getting just like Dubai," he said, referring to the abundance of competition in this market.

Curd of Qatar Airways, which will increase its Heathrow-Doha frequency to daily from May 21, also referred to the emirate when he said: "Rates to Dubai are so low that I won't be concentrating on selling the place."
Instead, he said, apart from Qatar - to which he felt he would devote some 75 percent of total ex-UK capacity - he would look at developing the onward Mideast markets of Abu Dhabi, Muscat and Jeddah.
To Doha, he said the bulk of shipments comprise oil industry-related equipment and stocks for hypermarkets spreading in Qatar.
Israel is a market which offers "very good cargo potential ex-UK", said Sarah price, senior route controller of wholesaler International Cargo Marketing.

She added that ICM had just started a new Heathrow-Tel Aviv consolidated service using El Al at 1.07 stg per kg/100 kg and will offer a cheaper alternative on Cyprus Airways at 1.03 stg from next month. - Reuters Air Cargo Service Tel +44 171 542 7706; fax 5017
